4782.prule: Every heavy syllable (VV or VC) is stressed; a light final syllable is never stressed; otherwise stress falls on every odd-numbered syllable counting from the left (the count restarting after a heavy syllable, cf. 'tau.-'ba.ba); the strongest stress is on the rightmost stressed syllable (a heavy final, else the penult or antepenult).

4783.prule: Tone language: underlying H vs Ø (toneless), tone-bearing unit = mora, melodic Hs assigned by mora counting. No word-stress rule is stated for Simbiti. 4784.prule: No word-stress rule is stated by any reachable source. Sukuma is described as a tone language with lexical and grammatical H/L/FR tone (Luhende 2018) and rightward H-tone displacement (Batibo 1991, Roberts 1992, Sietsema 1989, Goldsmith 1990, Matondo 2006). The only 'accent' statements are Herrmann 1898's pre-tonal acute/macron marks: the 'Ton' is a property of the verb stem (on its former penult, kept there when -ga is suffixed, so word antepenult in -túlaga), goes to a tense-prefix syllable (word antepenult) in Present 1 / Future only for verbs 'bei denen es sich bequem aussprechen lässt', and falls on the noun-final syllable before enclitic -ki; final syllables are 'mit Vehemenz herausgestossen' with a shortened final vowel. These placements do not reduce to a syllable-count position and are best read as H tone transcribed before tone was recognised.

4784.tone: Luhende 2018 p.25: 'Sukuma is a tonal language... three basic tones... H... L... FR... both lexical and grammatical tones.' Batibo 1991 (tone paper: nominals toneless 25% / shifted H 44% / fixed H 34%; two-directional LH melody spread) mentions stress only for loanwords: p.21 'The stress in this case was interpreted as a high tone in penultimate or final syllable'; p.23 'the H (representing stress in the language of origin) has surfaced on a short, usually penultimate vowel.' Roberts 1992, Sietsema 1989 (ch. 4), Goldsmith 1990 (pp.15-18), Matondo 2006: H surfaces displaced to the right of its underlying position (two syllables in Richardson's data, one in Goldsmith's); Sietsema's 'stress' is an abstract metrical head that attracts H, not phonetic word stress; none of them states word stress or penultimate lengthening. Herrmann 1898 (pre-tonal officer's grammar, no key to diacritics) marks 'Ton/Accent' with acutes, mostly on the stem or word penult (ku-túla, kw-ímba, múñhu, ssúdyi, múmbi, nugúti), kept on the stem under -ga (-túlaga, word antepenult), with macron-marked tense prefixes in Present 1 (n-dī-tula) called 'Accent auf die drittletzte Silbe' for some verbs, and on the noun-final syllable before -ki (múñhúki, ntíki: 'Der Accent fällt also auf die letzte Silbe des Substantivs und der Endvocal wird kurz', p.174); p.146 adds an emphatic final syllable with a shortened final vowel and 'Die Betonung ist sehr deutlich, nachdrücklich'.

tn.quote: Traditionally, Sukuma nominals have been tonally distinguished between the toned or marked and the toneless or unmarked at the underlying level. The toned nominals have again been differentiated between those associated with a fixed H and those associated with a shifted H (Richardson, 1959; Batibo, 1977/85). ... the TBU in Sukuma neither corresponds to the syllable nor to the mora. 4788.tone: Two-tone system (H / L) on every syllable, including minor syllables. Monosyllables carry lexical H or L; grammaticalised morphemes may lose lexical tone and take the polar-opposite tone of the morpheme to the left; functional morphemes may be lexically toneless and get a surface tone the same way; in an iambic foot the single lexical tone aligns with the major syllable and the minor syllable takes the polar-opposite tone (OCP, LL avoided); dual formation appears to flip the verb's tone sequence (abstract p. 97; secs. 7, 9.1-9.3). 'Stress' occurs only as the adjective 'unstressed' for minor syllables (p. 99) and in the phrase-level remark 'Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus' (p. 117), which is about emphasis/focus, not word stress. Data are from one elderly speaker of the Myebon dialect; the author warns (p. 98) that tones and vowels differ significantly between Sumtu dialects and that segmental phonology is outside the paper's scope.
4788.sec_quote: Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus, but pronominal verb prefixes are obligatorily attached to verbs in indicative statements (though not in negative statements or imperatives). 4789.heavy: A [+tense] vowel in the second syllable attracts main stress when the first syllable has a [-tense] vowel. Per the p. 10 feature table [tense] is + for å o u i̮ a e i and − for the short/lax ă ŏ ä̆ ö̆ ŭ and reduced ə; note 1 p. 10: 'A feszes magánhangzók időtartamukat tekintve hosszabbak a lazáknál. A legrövidebb a redukált ə magánhangzó.' (tense vowels are longer than lax ones; reduced ə is the shortest). So heavy = full (tense, longer) vowel; light = lax/short or reduced vowel. Codas play no stated role.
4789.dflt: first syllable (also when both σ1 and σ2 are full-vowelled)
4789.prule: Main word stress falls by default on the first syllable; when the first syllable has a [-tense] (lax/short, including reduced ə) vowel and the second syllable a [+tense] (full, longer) vowel, main stress shifts to the second syllable (səran 'Komi', səɣʌam 'my burbots', ḳŏrnat 'with a picture'). The 2017 edition gives only 'main stress mostly on the first syllable' and does not repeat the shift.
4789.srule: In words of more than three syllables a secondary stress falls on the third syllable (Csepregi 1998/2011 p. 14: ḳåtɣəʌamən, main σ1 + secondary σ3); the author's 2017 Russian edition generalises this to every odd-numbered syllable following the initial main stress (p. 58), i.e. binary alternation rightward from the main stress. Placement when the main stress has shifted to the second syllable is not stated.

4793.prule: Word-stress position is free and unpredictable (lexical): 'a posição da sílaba acentuada na palavra... parece ser livre' and 'não haver como predizer onde cairá o acento'. 4793.srule: None inside the word: isolated words carry one stress (degrees 0 átona / 1 tônica / 2 sentence nucleus, pp. 26-27; one mark per word in the lists pp. 28-29). 4793.tone: Suruí is tonal: 'A língua Suruí é tonal' (p. 24); two underlying tones /+ALT/ (H) and /-ALT/ (L), four surface pitch levels (extra-high, high, mid, low) produced by stress acting on tone (p. 24, rules RT1-RT6 pp. 25-26). Stress is a separate word property that usually but not always sits on an H syllable (p. 26). Corroboration, Bontkes, Carolyn (1988) A prosódia silábica suruí, Série Lingüística 9(2): 117-145, §1.3.4 'Acentuação', print pp. 123-124 (the section heading and its first sentences stand on p. 123; the two quoted sentences below stand on p. 124; 2007 online ed. p. 7): 'Geralmente, pode-se dizer que o acento cai num dos tons altos de uma palavra. Nas raízes verbais dissílabas, encontramos padrões tonais alto-baixo e baixo-alto, com acento na sílaba alta; enquanto nas raízes de tom baixo-baixo, o acento pode cair na primeira ou segunda sílaba.'... 'estes prefixos tendem a soar como acentuados quando ocorrem em palavras isoladas. A acentuação não tem função léxica na língua surui, mas parece influir nos padrões tonais, como se vê no caso dos substantivos possuídos.'. Bontkes thus denies a lexical (contrastive) function for stress but gives no positional rule either.

tn.quote: 1) A língua Suruí é tonal. Há poucas palavras que se distinguem entre si somente pelo tom, mas mesmo assim existe a necessidade de se considerar o tom como uma característica importante desta língua. Na superfície percebemos quatro tons que, na estrutura profunda, se reduzem a dois. Fonéticamente temos tom extra-alto [V̋], alto [V́], médio [V̄] e baixo [V̀] com os traços, [4ALT], [3ALT], [2ALT] e [1ALT], respectivamente; podemos mostrar que estes tons resultam da ação da acentuação sobre dois tons distintivos /V́/ [+ALT] e /V̀/ [-ALT].
tn.translation: 1) The Suruí language is tonal. There are few words distinguished from one another by tone alone, but even so tone must be considered an important characteristic of this language. On the surface we perceive four tones which, in deep structure, reduce to two. Phonetically we have extra-high, high, mid and low tone with the features [4ALT], [3ALT], [2ALT] and [1ALT] respectively; we can show that these tones result from the action of stress on two distinctive tones /V́/ [+ALT] and /V̀/ [-ALT].
tn.cite: van der Meer, Tine H. (1982). Fonologia da língua Suruí. Dissertação de Mestrado (orient. Aryon D. Rodrigues), Instituto de Estudos da Linguagem, Universidade Estadual de Campinas, 75 pp.
tn.locator: p. 24, Ch. III 'A sílaba', §B 'Tom e acentuação
tn.note: Two distinctive level tones (high, low) on each syllable; four phonetic levels (extra-high, high, mid, low) derived from stress degree acting on tone. Word stress is separate, free and contrastive.

4794.dq: In words of two syllables the accent is usually placed on the first syllable ... In words of three syllables, if they are simple words, the accent is on the antepenult ... In compound words the accent retains the place it has in the simple words.
4794.dloc: Douglin 1887, Introduction (intended for the teacher), section 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7.
4794.prule: Douglin 1887 (pre-tonal reading primer): the accent is 'usually' on the first syllable of disyllables and on the antepenult, i.e. the first syllable, of simple trisyllables; in compound words 'the accent retains the place it has in the simple words' (Douglin does not say whether a compound then carries one accent or several). Every modern description reached (Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013; Sangster & Faber 1968) describes Susu as a tone language (H, HL, LH melodies on mono- and disyllabic nouns, mora as TBU; five tone types per vowel in the pedagogical course) and states no stress or accent rule.
4794.srule: Not mentioned in Douglin 1887, Introduction 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7 (the section gives only the disyllable and simple-trisyllable accent and a sentence on compounds). Houis 1963 (ch. II section 35 fn. 1, p. 29) denies word accent altogether: 'le susu est une langue qui ne connaît que les tons et non l'accent'.
4794.quote: In words of two syllables the accent is usually placed on the first syllable: as "male" ("rice") = "má-le"; "bende" ("dirt") = "bén-de"; "kubbe" ("ashes" or "dust") = "kúb-be"; "heri" ("peace") = "hé-ri." In words of three syllables, if they are simple words, the accent is on the antepenult: as "hárrige" ("lot" or "portion"); "yámmine" ("a kingdom"); "béllaχe" ("a hand"); "wéllaχe" ("a wooden slate"). In compound words the accent retains the place it has in the simple words.
4794.loc: Douglin 1887, Introduction (intended for the teacher), section 'ACCENT', pp. 6-7; Green et al. 2013, section 1 'Basics of Susu nominal tone', paragraph 4; Sangster & Faber 1968, pre-speech unit 'Tones / Les tons'.

4794.tone: Green, Anderson & Obeng 2013, section 1 para. 4: "Previous work on Susu (e.g. Grégoire 1978; Houis 1963; Touré 1994, 2004) converges on the fact that mono- and disyllabic nouns, generally speaking, have one of three distinct tonal melodies, namely H, HL, and LH." Examples (1): /HH/ [túlí] 'ear', /HL/ [kérì] 'hoe', /LH/ [ɡìnɛ̀] 'woman'; TBU = mora. The words 'stress'/'accent' occur in this paper only in a bibliography title (Bamba 1991), in the tone-marking convention (acute = H, grave = L) and in footnote 10 on foot-head prominence in Bambara; nothing is said about stress or accent in Susu. Sangster & Faber 1968, 'Tones' (scan): "Just as different sounds are used to keep words apart, so are different tones used..."; five tones per vowel (neutral/mid, high, low, high-falling, low-rising) with sentence intonation superimposed; no word-stress statement (the French 'l'accentuation sur la dernière syllabe' concerns the tone that distinguishes agent from action nominals). Douglin's 1887 'accent' predates any tonal analysis: his "má-le" 'rice' puts the accent on the syllable that is L in the modern /LH/ analysis (Green et al. cite /mààlé/-type LH nouns), so it is not a rendering of H tone.

4797.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable by default (syllabic trochees built left to right, leftmost foot is the head). Disyllables: initial stress whatever the weights (LL 'home', 'potato'; LH 'pillow', 'love'; HL huk.na 'thin', 'hate'; HH 'brinjal', 'name of Bengali month'; p. 149). Trisyllables: antepenult (initial) unless the antepenult is light and the penult heavy (closed), in which case the penult takes primary stress (LHH 'prize', LHL 'examination'; pp. 146-147, 151-152); the final syllable never carries primary stress. Heavy = closed syllable only (VC, CVC, CVVC); vowel length is not distinctive; diphthongs are monomoraic (pp. 140, 145). Data are monomorphemic, non-compound di- and trisyllables only (native words of 4-5 syllables 'very rare', p. 139). Author's parameters (p. 148): Foot type Trochee / Direction Left-to-right / Word Dominance Head Left / Quantity-sensitive 'Yes and no (Partially quantity sensitive)' / Extrametricality Yes. Transcription caveat: the PDF drops the special IPA glyphs in the example words, so only the weight patterns, glosses and stress positions are verifiable from the text; the pointed forms (ba.ɽi 'home', ba.liʃ 'pillow', baiŋ.gɔn 'brinjal') are read from p. 149.
4797.srule: Two degrees of stress. In trisyllables with an initial primary foot, a word-final heavy (closed) syllable forms its own foot and carries secondary stress: LLH ('LL)(H) 'dawn', 'fool'; HHH ('HH)(H) 'reservation' (summary table p. 156 also lists HLH ('HL)(H)). No secondary stress on a final light syllable (('LL)L 'pink', ('HL)L 'alum', ('HH)L 'property': extrametrical) nor on the final heavy of LHH (L('HH) 'prize': 'the final heavy syllable cannot form a separate foot to avoid stress clash'). Words of four or more syllables not analysed.

4799.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the root ('por lo general'); monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes of verbs and nouns are unstressed; when an aspect prefix fuses with a vowel-initial root the fused word-initial syllable takes the stress (ga-+aza-beß > gázabeß); disyllabic prefixes/affixes bear their own stress on their first syllable, so a word with polysyllabic affixes can carry two or three stresses; Spanish loans keep the Spanish stress position. Position is set by root/affix identity, not by syllable count or weight.
4799.srule: Additional stresses are morphologically placed: each disyllabic prefix/affix (xele-, gule-, xulu-, belexe-, dxele-, -técaze-) carries its own stress on its first syllable (unwritten), so a word with polysyllabic affixes has two or three stressed syllables (Dxéle-dá-lýn-técaze-beß-baß); no primary-vs-secondary ranking is given and no rhythmic/alternating stress is described; words without polysyllabic affixes have one stressed syllable.

4799.exq_: El acento prosódico por lo general cae en la primera sílaba de la raíz. [...] Los préstamos del español al zapoteco conservan el acento en la misma sílaba que en español. Ejemplos: mal -tý -dxa mucho más peor máltýdxaß; burro -dauß burrito búrrodauß
4799.tone: The language is lexically tonal, but the sketch has no tone section and treats tone only in passing: fn. 9 p. 48 'Los símbolos (a) y (b) refieren a tonos altos y bajos' (distinguishing otherwise homographic verb roots -uti- (a)/(b)); fn. p. 103 '(b.m.) refiere a tonos (bajo-medio) mientras que (b.b.) refiere a tonos (bajo-bajo)' on numerals; polar questions in future/present are formed 'con un tono alto en el sílabo acentuado' (p. 63), i.e. tone is realised on the stressed syllable. The stress rule is stated independently of tone, so the record is set by morphology with a tone flag rather than tone or pitch accent.

In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone (oxutéexa ‘to cook’) and before the penult a long H syllable is level-H (oxutééxela ‘to cook for’). Rising tones always become level H, so underlying /oxu-íra/ undergoes glide forma…
4800.dloc: Odden, David. 2015. Bantu Phonology. Oxford Handbooks Online in Linguistics, doi:10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199935345.013.59 [author's draft, the Internet Archive 2016-07-04], p. 22 (tone-contour passage)
4800.prule: Tone language: H vs. L/toneless with one tone per mora; falling contour only on long syllables (long H penult falls, long H before the penult is level); verb tone = lexical /H/ vs. toneless root plus tense-determined melodic H. No stress or accent rule stated.
4800.quote: Some allow contour tones only on long syllables, for example Hausa and many Bantu languages (Tachoni, Dembwa Taita) have just falling tone (F) and only on long syllables. ... In these languages, short syllables can only have level tone. Languages like Tachoni, which limit tones to one-per-mora, are “contourless” in the moraic sense, but from the syllabic perspective, they allow contours. In contrast, Miya has long vowels but no R or F, and Tachoni still has only one of the expected contours on long vowels.
4800.loc: quote: Odden 2020 draft pp. 3-4, section 3.2.2 'Contours'; and: Odden 2015 draft p. 22 (tone-contour passage) and p. 28 ex. (58)
4800.tone: Both Odden drafts treat Tachoni purely as a tone language: H vs. L per mora, falling tone only on long syllables (and only F, not R: 'Tachoni still has only one of the expected contours on long vowels'); long H penults fall while a long H syllable before the penult is level. Odden 2015 draft p. 22 (verbatim): 'In Tachoni, long penults with H have falling tone (oxutéexa ‘to cook’) and before the penult a long H syllable is level-H (oxutééxela ‘to cook for’). Rising tones always become level H, so underlying /oxu-íra/ undergoes glide formation which should yield oxwiíra, but this surfaces as [oxwííra] ‘to kill’. This gives rise to a limited derivational contrast between level H versus fall on the penult.' The word 'stress' does not occur in the 2015 Bantu Phonology draft (a full-text search count 0) and occurs in the 2020 draft only for Swahili (line 29, 'a continuum between tone (e.g. Ewe) and stress (e.g. Swahili)') and in reference titles; 'accent' only as the acute-accent notation for H and in reference titles. No statement about word stress, accent or penultimate prominence in Tachoni in any source opened (Odden 2020/2015 drafts, Odden AfricanTone earlier draft, Marlo 2013, Wanjala 2014).

4801.dq: In Tafi, the syllable is a tone bearing unit and it may be made up of an onset and a peak; a peak; or a peak and a coda. [...] The peak which always carries a tone consists of a vowel or a syllabic nasal and it is the most sonorous element in the syllable and it is also the one required component of the syllable.
4801.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology: sec. 2.1 Syllable structure, book p.15
4801.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. Tafi is described as a tone language: three level tones (L, M, H) plus five contour tones (HM, HL, ML, LM, LH); the syllable is the tone-bearing unit and every syllable peak carries a tone; tone is contrastive lexically (verb and noun minimal pairs) and grammatically. The grammar contains no statement on stress or accent anywhere.
4801.quote: [p.15, 2.1 Syllable structure] In Tafi, the syllable is a tone bearing unit and it may be made up of an onset and a peak; a peak; or a peak and a coda. The peak which always carries a tone consists of a vowel or a syllabic nasal and it is the most sonorous element in the syllable and it is also the one required component of the syllable. [...] [p.32, 2.4 Tone] Tone plays a significant role in Tafi and many other African languages. 4801.idn: Tafi (autonym Tɨgbɔ; people Baagbɔ), spoken in the four communities Agɔme, Abuiƒe, Madɔ and Atome; data gathered mainly from Madɔ, with recordings from Agɔme/Abuiƒe flagged where different; 'Dialect differentiation in Tafi seems to be minimal' (p.8).; data: Two field trips to Tafi…
4801.tone: Sec. 2.4 (pp.32-33): three level tones L, M, H and contour tones HM, HL, ML, LM, LH realised on one syllable peak; syllable = TBU (p.15, fn.: a syllabic N 'always bears a tone'); tone functions lexically and syntactically (2.4.1 tone patterns in verbs and nouns, 2.4.2 grammatical tone). 4803.prule: No Tagbu-specific stress statement exists. The only accent statement in the sole grammar of Tagbu is a group-level one for 'these languages, especially of Ndogo', offered as 'suggestions (I shall not call them rules)' and 'a guide for Ndogo': monosyllables unproblematic; polysyllables are mostly compounds whose every component 'must have its own accent duly stressed'; disyllables have either 'an even stress on both syllables' or 'a real accent on the first' (the latter = words with l, r, n in the second syllable, whose vowel is often lost: mbòro = mbòò, kóró = kóó); 'the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables' (p. 29), so reduplications carry accents on syllables 1 and 3 (exception mbulàmbulà). Remark V extends the remarks by name to Bviri only; Tagbu (Tangbu) is never named in secs. 4-5 (pp. 15-33). The languages are described as tonal with four levels (low, mid, high, very high, p. 17). No fixed, syllable-count-computable, quantity-insensitive stress position is stated for Tagbu or for the group.

4806.tone: Source-level: tone, not stress. Sec. 4 opens 'The issue of prosodic pitch, whether tone or stress, in Tagoi (or in other Rashad languages) has been the subject of different opinions'; reviews MacDiarmid 1931 (tone recorded in Moreb), Meinhof 1916 (no trace of tone), Stevenson 1956/57: 47 and 1964: 86 (stress 'plays a marked role and may be responsible for grammatical and lexical contrast'); then attests a two-tone H/L contrast on mono- and disyllabic nouns and concludes 'it might be that Stevenson noticed the pitch distinction but he attributed it to stress'. Both morae of a long vowel bear the same tone (HH or LL); no phonemic contour tones; phonetic HL fall only on word-final long syllables, never on monosyllables (Table 13); rising tone unattested. Possible grammatical tone LL > LH in a few plurals (Table 11) is judged doubtful because prefixation and final-vowel shortening co-occur. evidence_works.work: Donaldson 1963, White Tai phonology (M.A. thesis, Hartford Seminary Foundation, Hartford CT = Hartford Studies in Linguistics 5: iii+50 pp.; SIL Language & Culture Archives 9514)
evidence_works.detail: Field data gathered by the author at the White Tai refugee village of Tung Nghia (Lai Chau dialect) from April 1960 to October 1961 under SIL auspices, principal informant Mrs. Dieu Nang Zane (p. 2 and n. 2); stress observations come from her tapes. Sec. 1.5 'Emphatic stress' (p. 36): 'A slight lengthening of the syllable utterance final is normal. Emphatic stress consists of extra loudness and of lengthening of the vowel and the final sonorant, if there is one; it occurs on syllables utterance finally or medially. On the mid-low and mid tones the pitch may be slightly higher than normally.'... 'The preceding remarks are based on very limited occurrences of the phenomena in my tapes. Further study will be required to confirm the observations made thus far and to make possible a detailed description of stress, intonation, and juncture.' Sec. 1.1 (p. 5): 'The syllable structure in White Tai is identical with its morpheme structure. Only six two-syllable items have been observed in which neither syllable could be identified as a morpheme.' Sec. 1.41 (p. 25) notes that emphatic stress affects some tone allophones. The work describes only emphatic (utterance-level) prominence and utterance-final lengthening on a tone language with monosyllabic morphemes; it gives no word-level stress placement rule and does not conflict with Gedney 1989 [1964].
